implementation_notes: `@dataclass(frozen=True)` makes instances immutable (assignment raises FrozenInstanceError) and `dataclasses.replace(obj, field=value)` builds the updated copy through `__init__`, so one level of update is a function call and depth nests - `replace(p, home=replace(p.home, city="Berlin"))` - which replaces the hand-written copy. The two dominant third-party data layers provide the same idiom (`attrs.evolve`, pydantic's `model_copy(update=...)`, which deliberately skips validation), and all three are still name-based rather than composable. A real lens - a getter/setter pair carried as a value, e.g. python-lenses' `Lens(getter, setter)` with `.set(v)(state)` composition - is justified when a path must be stored, derived from configuration or reused across modules; for one field in one place, `replace()` is shorter and dependency-free.
pitfalls: `replace()` calls `__init__` again, so `__post_init__` side effects re-run and `init=False` fields are re-initialised instead of copied - the "copy" can differ from the original in ways the source code does not show.
`frozen=True` is shallow: a list/dict field is still mutable in place, which both breaks the immutability discipline and poisons the generated `__hash__`.
Everything is name-based and dynamic: renaming a field breaks the update at runtime, and no type checker flags a `replace(..., city=...)` that now targets a different field.
